message.content:
The entire cli uses a contextinjector to add context how the entire cli is used. The
  injected context looks like this "Entire is enabled for this repo. Run entire
  agent-help to see what entire does and which subcommand to use, then entire agent-help
  <command> for that command's exact, current flags. Commits automatically capture the AI
  session as a checkpoint, so never create checkpoints by hand — just commit normally.
  Before large edits, entire why <file>:<line> and entire checkpoint search recover the
  intent behind existing code. Leave setup and destructive commands (enable, disable,
  clean, rewind, auth) to the user. This repo is auto-detected from the git origin remote
  as gh/acme/app; you are already inside it, so never ask the user for the repo name."
  Can you search all claude sessions on this machine if "entire why" or "entire
  checkpoint search" was actually used?

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- entire-engineering:design:design-implementation-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to verify that a UI implementation matches its Figma design specifications. This agent should be called after code has been written to implement a design, particularly after HTML/CSS/React components have been created or modified. The agent will visually compare the live implementation against the Figma design and provide detailed feedback on discrepancies.

Examples:
- <example>
  Context: The user has just implemented a new component based on a Figma design.
  user: "I've finished implementing the hero section based on the Figma design"
  assistant: "I'll review how well your implementation matches the Figma design."
  <commentary>
  Since UI implementation has been completed, use the design-implementation-reviewer agent to compare the live version with Figma.
  </commentary>
  </example>
- <example>
  Context: After the general code agent has implemented design changes.
  user: "Update the button styles to match the new design system"
  assistant: "I've updated the button styles. Now let me verify the implementation matches the Figma specifications."
  <commentary>
  After implementing design changes, proactively use the design-implementation-reviewer to ensure accuracy.
  </commentary>
  </example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:design:design-iterator: Use this agent PROACTIVELY when design work isn't coming together on the first attempt. If you've made 1-2 design changes and the result still feels off, suggest using this agent with 5x or 10x iterations for deeper refinement. This agent takes screenshots, analyzes what's not working, implements improvements, and repeats N times to systematically fix design issues. Perfect when colors feel wrong, layouts aren't balanced, or the overall aesthetic needs work that single changes can't achieve. <example>Context: User asks to change button color but result still looks off. user: "Change the button to blue" assistant: [makes change, takes screenshot] "The button is now blue, but I notice the overall color balance still feels off. Would you like me to use the design-iterator agent with 5 iterations to systematically improve the color harmony and visual balance?" <commentary>PROACTIVE USE: After a simple change doesn't fully resolve the design issue, suggest the design-iterator to do deeper work.</commentary></example> <example>Context: User's design request leads to something that doesn't look right. user: "Make the hero section more modern" assistant: [makes initial changes] "I've added some modern elements, but the result isn't quite coming together. This looks like it needs iterative refinement. Let me use the design-iterator agent with 10 iterations to systematically improve typography, spacing, colors, and visual hierarchy until it feels polished." <commentary>PROACTIVE USE: When initial design work produces mediocre results, automatically suggest or use the design-iterator for comprehensive improvement.</commentary></example> <example>Context: User wants explicit iterative refinement. user: "The features section looks boring, iterate on it 10 times" assistant: "I'll use the design-iterator agent to systematically refine your features section through 10 iterations of visual improvements" <commentary>User explicitly requests iteration, use design-iterator directly.</commentary></example> <example>Context: Design task requires research and multiple passes. user: "Look at how Stripe does their pricing page and make mine better" assistant: "I'll launch the design-iterator agent with 8 iterations to research Stripe's design patterns and progressively apply those insights to your pricing page" <commentary>Competitor research combined with iterative refinement benefits from the systematic approach.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

The agent excels at synthesizing information from multiple sources to provide comprehensive guidance on how to implement features or solve problems according to industry standards. <example>Context: User wants to know the best way to structure GitHub issues for their Rails project. user: "I need to create some GitHub issues for our project. Can you research best practices for writing good issues?" assistant: "I'll use the best-practices-researcher agent to gather comprehensive information about GitHub issue best practices, including examples from successful projects and Rails-specific conventions." <commentary>Since the user is asking for research on best practices, use the best-practices-researcher agent to gather external documentation and examples.</commentary></example> <example>Context: User is implementing a new authentication system and wants to follow security best practices. user: "We're adding JWT authentication to our Rails API. - entire-engineering:review:data-integrity-guardian: Use this agent when you need to review database migrations, data models, or any code that manipulates persistent data. This includes checking migration safety, validating data constraints, ensuring transaction boundaries are correct, and verifying that referential integrity and privacy requirements are maintained. <example>Context: The user has just written a database migration that adds a new column and updates existing records. user: "I've created a migration to add a status column to the orders table" assistant: "I'll use the data-integrity-guardian agent to review this migration for safety and data integrity concerns" <commentary>Since the user has created a database migration, use the data-integrity-guardian agent to ensure the migration is safe, handles existing data properly, and maintains referential integrity.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user has implemented a service that transfers data between models. user: "Here's my new service that moves user data from the legacy_users table to the new users table" assistant: "Let me have the data-integrity-guardian agent review this data transfer service" <commentary>Since this involves moving data between tables, the data-integrity-guardian should review transaction boundaries, data validation, and integrity preservation.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:review:data-migration-expert: Use this agent when reviewing PRs that touch database migrations, data backfills, or any code that transforms production data. This agent validates ID mappings against production reality, checks for swapped values, verifies rollback safety, and ensures data integrity during schema changes. Essential for any migration that involves ID mappings, column renames, or data transformations. <example>Context: The user has a PR with database migrations that involve ID mappings. user: "Review this PR that migrates from action_id to action_module_name" assistant: "I'll use the data-migration-expert agent to validate the ID mappings and migration safety" <commentary>Since the PR involves ID mappings and data migration, use the data-migration-expert to verify the mappings match production and check for swapped values.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user has a migration that transforms enum values. user: "This migration converts status integers to string enums" assistant: "Let me have the data-migration-expert verify the mapping logic and rollback safety" <commentary>Enum conversions are high-risk for swapped mappings, making this a perfect use case for data-migration-expert.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:review:deployment-verification-agent: Use this agent when a PR touches production data, migrations, or any behavior that could silently discard or duplicate records. Produces a concrete pre/post-deploy checklist with SQL verification queries, rollback procedures, and monitoring plans. Essential for risky data changes where you need a Go/No-Go decision. <example>Context: The user has a PR that modifies how emails are classified. user: "This PR changes the classification logic, can you create a deployment checklist?" assistant: "I'll use the deployment-verification-agent to create a Go/No-Go checklist with verification queries" <commentary>Since the PR affects production data behavior, use deployment-verification-agent to create concrete verification and rollback plans.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user is deploying a migration that backfills data. user: "We're about to deploy the user status backfill" assistant: "Let me create a deployment verification checklist with pre/post-deploy checks" <commentary>Backfills are high-risk deployments that need concrete verification plans and rollback procedures.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

## Answer: neither was ever actually run — 0 invocations

I parsed all 174 transcript files in `~/.claude/projects` (133 distinct sessions, ~33k records, **6,274 Bash tool calls**) rather than grepping, because the injected hint quotes both commands verbatim in every prompt — a text grep is ~100% false positives.

| Command | Real invocations |
|---|---|
| `entire why` | **0** |
| `entire checkpoint search` (and `cp`/`checkpoints` aliases) | **0** |
| `entire search` (top-level shortcut) | **0** |

### What the textual matches actually were

- **`entire why`** — 4 matches: two are `labs.go` source (`Invocation: "entire why"`) read by a subagent, two are this conversation.
- **`entire checkpoint search`** — 35 matches: 33 are diffs of the `cmd.Example` string in `search_cmd.go` and `agent-help` output captured as tool results; 2 are this conversation.
- **`entire search`** — 7 Bash matches, all prose *inside* commands, never in command position: `entire trail finding add --body '...'`, a `git commit -F -` heredoc, and a `gh pr create --body` for the cross-repo explain PR.

### Denominator

25 transcript files carried the injected hint (2026-07-07 → 2026-08-11). What agents *did* run in exactly those sessions:

```
185  entire trail (finding/show/update/list/…)
 22  entire agent-help
 16  entire api
 16  entire hooks
 10  entire checkpoint explain
  6  entire status
  0  entire why
  0  entire checkpoint search
```

So agents *do* act on the first sentence of the injection (`agent-help` → 22 calls, and it fans out into `api`/`trail`/`status`). The third sentence — the `why` / `checkpoint search` recommendation — has a 0% hit rate. Notably, the 10 `checkpoint explain` calls all cluster in one hour on 2026-08-10, i.e. you testing the `--repo` feature you were building, not organic recall use.

Your `~/.zsh_history` agrees: `entire search` once by hand, `entire why` never.

**Caveats:** the hint only appears in 25 of 174 files, so most sessions predate it; `~/.zsh_history` is only 20KB and is a partial record. I checked non-Bash invocation shapes too (all string fields of every tool input, `./entire`, `$BIN`, `go run ./cmd/entire`) — no command-position matches anywhere. I scanned Claude Code only, as asked; `~/.codex`, `~/.gemini`, `~/.cursor`, `~/.copilot`, `~/.factory`, `~/.opencode`, and `~/.pi` all exist on this machine and are unscanned.

Saved the finding to memory, since it bears on how you word the context injector.

The actionable read: **`agent-help` converts, the recall commands don't.** The injection's first sentence produced 22 calls and fanned out into `api`/`trail`/`status`; the sentence recommending `entire why` and `entire checkpoint search` produced nothing in 25 hint-bearing sessions over five weeks. That's a wording/discoverability signal, not a signal about the commands — plausibly because "before large edits" is a trigger condition an agent has to *notice it's in*, whereas "run `entire agent-help`" is an unconditional instruction it can execute immediately.

44	    """Drop heredoc bodies: their lines are data, not commands."""

58	    """Blank out quoted spans so prose inside --body '...' can't look like a

content.text:
Works across all six agent CLIs now: 963 transcripts, 447k records, 12,275 shell calls. Same answer — **0 and 0** — but on ~5× the evidence.

One correction to my earlier numbers: I reported 10 `entire checkpoint explain` calls. The real count is 6 (4 in Claude Code). The extra four were heredoc'd help text from `explain.go` being written, which my ad-hoc scan scored as invocations — exactly the class of bug the hardened script fixes.

## Why it took so many loops

Four specific mistakes, each now preventable:

| Loop cost | Mistake | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 2 loops | Guessed the injected-hint string, got 0 matches | Grep a short distinctive substring first |
| 2 loops | Assumed hook context lives in `message.content` — it doesn't | Test the **raw line**, not a parsed field |
| 1 loop | Hardcoded Claude's `tool_use → input.command` path | Discover command-bearing keys empirically |
| 1 loop | No heredoc/quote handling → 7 false `entire search` hits | Strip heredocs, mask quotes, then split |

## Option A: skip the agent entirely (0 loops)

`agent_cmd_usage.py` is stdlib-only, one file, and now encodes all four fixes:

```bash
python3 agent_cmd_usage.py --hint "Entire is enabled for this repo" --all-verbs \
    entire "entire why" "entire checkpoint search" "entire search"
```

It's at `…/scratchpad/agent_cmd_usage.py`. Say the word and I'll commit it to the repo so it's on every machine — that seems like the real answer to "another machine."

## Option B: the improved prompt

```
Measure whether agents ever actually RAN `entire why` or `entire checkpoint
search` on this machine.

TRAP: a UserPromptSubmit hook injects context quoting both commands verbatim
into every prompt, and both also appear in the CLI's own source, help output,
and PR bodies. A text grep is ~100% false positives. Only count a command in
shell COMMAND POSITION inside a tool call's command field.

Do this in ONE pass — no exploratory greps:
1. Transcripts: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl (includes subagents). Also
   ~/.codex, ~/.copilot, ~/.factory, ~/.gemini, ~/.opencode, ~/.pi if present.
2. DISCOVER the schema, don't assume it: dump which key names hold shell
   commands across a sample. Recurse generically over those keys. Do not
   hardcode one agent's message.content[] -> tool_use -> input.command path;
   Codex stores argv lists like ["bash","-lc","..."] under `command`.
3. Normalize before matching: strip heredoc bodies, blank quoted spans, split
   on `; && || | newline`, strip leading FOO=bar / sudo / `cd x &&`. Match only
   at the START of a resulting segment.
4. Never match tool RESULTS or stdout — help text and diffs live there.
5. Denominator: count transcripts containing the injected hint by testing a
   short distinctive substring against the RAW LINE, not a parsed field. The
   hook context is not stored under message.content.

Deliver:
- real invocation count per target command, with every matching command line
  shown so I can eyeball it
- how many transcripts carried the hint, plus date range
- a census of every `entire <verb>` that WAS invoked (what agents reach for
  instead)
- an explicit list of what you did not scan
```

The load-bearing parts are the TRAP paragraph and step 5 — those two alone would have cut this from eight loops to about three.

content.text:
No. Verified just now — that run had cwd `/tmp` and produced identical results.

**Why cwd is irrelevant:** the script resolves `~/.claude/projects` and the five other agent roots via `expanduser`, all absolute. It never opens a repo file, never shells out to `git` or `entire`. The project *path* is encoded in the transcript directory name (`-Users-soph-Work-entire-devenv-cli`), so all repos' sessions are visible from anywhere — that's why the scan found `cli`, `cli_experiments`, `cli_experiments_2`, `entire-io`, `go-git` and the rest regardless of where I stood.

**The contamination test is the interesting result:**

```
this session's transcript
  raw grep "entire why"        → 29 hits
  command-position scan        → 0 hits
```

The hardened method is self-immune: `python3 agent_cmd_usage.py … "entire why"` doesn't match because the segment starts with `python3`, and the quoted arg gets blanked by `mask_quotes`. The naive grep method degrades every time you run the analysis — each run injects ~30 more decoys into the corpus for whoever greps next.

**Two places the repo does matter:**

1. **Committing the script.** That's the only genuinely repo-bound step, and it's the real answer to "another machine" — a copy in the cli repo travels with the clone.
2. **Checkpoint-index pollution, if Entire is enabled where you run it.** The transcript scan doesn't read git, so it's unaffected. But if you commit in that repo afterwards, this session condenses into `entire/checkpoints/v1` and gets pushed — so `entire checkpoint search "entire why"` will start returning *this analysis*. Mildly funny, mildly annoying if you later want a clean read on that index. Running from a repo without Entire enabled, or just not committing, avoids it.

So: run it from `~` or anywhere convenient. The only prompt input that's product-specific is the `--hint` substring, and `"Entire is enabled for this repo"` is stable across repos.

Want me to commit `agent_cmd_usage.py` into the cli repo? `scripts/` or `hack/` would be the natural home — say which and I'll open a branch.

+// agentHelpAudience answers the question an agent actually has when it reads this
+// listing: may I run this without being asked? A flat alphabetical dump of every
+// command cannot answer it, so an agent either runs nothing or runs something it
+// should have left alone (`entire enable`, `entire review`, `entire org create`).
+// Grouping by initiator puts that judgment in the CLI, where it is maintained
+// once, rather than in each agent's guesswork or in the first-turn injection,
+// which pays for it on every session.
+  // agentHelpAudienceReadOnly: inspection only. Safe to run unprompted whenever
+  // it would inform the work; cannot change repo, account, or Entire state.
+  // agentHelpAudienceTaskDriven: part of doing the work, but it writes data or
+  // spends tokens. Run when the task calls for it, not speculatively.
+  // agentHelpAudienceUserOwned: setup, auth, account/admin, or destructive. The
+  // agent may suggest these but must not run them on its own initiative.
+// agentHelpAudiences classifies every advertised top-level command. It is a
+// single table rather than a per-command Annotations field so the whole policy
+// is reviewable in one place — the classification is a judgment call and reads
+// as one only when the commands sit side by side.
+// Unlisted commands fall back to agentHelpAudienceUserOwned (see
+// agentHelpAudienceFor): the fail-safe direction is an agent declining to run
+// something it could have, never running something it should not have.
+// top-level command lands unclassified, so the fallback is a backstop and not
+  // Writes data or spends tokens; task-driven.
+  // The user's: setup, auth, account/admin, destructive.
+// agentHelpAudienceSections renders in this order: what an agent may do on its
+// own first, what it must not do last.
+  {agentHelpAudienceReadOnly, "Safe to run on your own — read-only, changes nothing:", "read-only"},
+  {agentHelpAudienceTaskDriven, "Run when the task calls for it — writes data or spends tokens:", "task-driven"},
+  {agentHelpAudienceUserOwned, "The user's to run — suggest it, don't run it (setup, auth, admin, destructive):", "user-owned"},
+// agentHelpAudienceFor classifies one command, defaulting unlisted commands to
+// user-owned so an unclassified addition is under- rather than over-advertised.
+// agentHelpAudienceSlug is the stable machine-readable form emitted in --json,
+// so an agent parsing the structured output gets the same guidance as one
+// reading the text (the repo's agent-safe-fallback rule).
// newAgentHelpCmd builds the `entire agent-help` command. It is visible in

one command's current flags; `--json` emits structured output. It is the single
source of truth the first-turn context injection and the `--agent-help-skill`
skill point agents at, instead of enumerating a surface that goes stale.

The bare listing is grouped by **who should initiate the command**, not
alphabetically, because the question an agent has when reading it is "may I run
this unprompted?" — read-only (safe on its own) · task-driven (writes data or
spends tokens) · user-owned (setup, auth, admin, destructive: suggest, never
run). The classification lives in one reviewable table,
`agentHelpAudiences` in `agent_help_cmd.go`, and is mirrored into `--json` as an
`audience` field on top-level commands so structured consumers get the same
guidance. Two rules matter when editing it: the listing is group-granular, so a
group counts as read-only **only if every advertised subcommand is** (`checkpoint`
and `session` read as read-only but are not — `checkpoint policy` updates policy,
`session` carries adopt/attach/resume/stop); and an unclassified command defaults
to user-owned, with `TestAgentHelpAudiences_CoverEveryAdvertisedCommand` failing
CI so a new command cannot ship unclassified.

injection used to recommend "before large edits", against 25 calls to the
agent-help pointer in the same corpus — the recommendation only cost first-turn
tokens, and framed a sometimes-appropriate query as an always-do step. The
injection carries only invariants that hold on every turn.

Both changes are in and the full CI suite is green.

## 1. Injected context, trimmed

Removed the sentence your data indicted:

```diff
- Before large edits, `entire why <file>:<line>` and `entire checkpoint search`
- recover the intent behind existing code.
```

What's left is only what holds on **every** turn — the agent-help pointer (25 measured calls), the auto-capture invariant, the setup/destructive guardrail, and the repo name. That's ~150 characters off the first turn of every session, and it drops the framing problem you named: a sometimes-appropriate query stated as an always-do step.

## 2. agent-help, grouped by who initiates

It was a flat alphabetical dump of 33 commands, which can't answer the only question an agent has when reading it — *may I run this unprompted?* Now:

```
  Safe to run on your own — read-only, changes nothing:
    activity, blame, experts, labs, recap, search, status, tokens, version, why

  Run when the task calls for it — some subcommands write data or spend tokens:
    api, checkpoint, dispatch, doctor, import, investigate, review, runner, session, trail

  The user's to run — suggest it, don't run it (setup, auth, admin, destructive):
    agent, auth, clean, configure, disable, enable, grant, login, logout, org,
    plugin, project, repo
```

Ordering is load-bearing (may-do first, must-not last), and `--json` carries an `audience` field so structured consumers get the same answer.

**Two judgment calls worth your review**, both in the one table `agentHelpAudiences`:

- **`checkpoint` and `session` are *not* read-only.** I had them there initially. `checkpoint policy` is "Inspect and **update**", and `session` carries `adopt/attach/resume/stop`. Since the listing is group-granular, a group is read-only only if *every* advertised subcommand is — otherwise the heading is a promise the drill-down contradicts. There's a regression test naming both.
- **`review` and `investigate` are task-driven, not user-owned.** They spawn multi-agent runs that cost real money. I judged "run when the task calls for it" correct because they're legitimate work, but if you'd rather an agent never start one unprompted, moving them to user-owned is a one-line change.

Unclassified commands default to user-owned, and `TestAgentHelpAudiences_CoverEveryAdvertisedCommand` fails CI if a new command ships without a tier — so this can't silently rot.

I confirmed they're on `main` with my work stashed, so they're not from this change and I left them alone — but they will fail CI on this branch too. Want me to fix them here, or keep this branch clean and file them separately?

content.text:
Both changes are in, full CI green.

## Read-only subcommands broken out

The table is now keyed by command *path*, so the eight safe subcommands inside the two task-driven groups surface directly in the allow list:

```
  Safe to run on your own — read-only, changes nothing:
    …
    checkpoint explain   checkpoint list   checkpoint search   checkpoint tokens
    session current      session info      session list        session tokens
```

The groups themselves stay under "run when the task calls for it" (they still carry `checkpoint policy` and `session adopt/attach/resume/stop`), so nothing under the read-only heading is a false promise. Mutating siblings are classified too but stay collapsed — the listing answers "what may I run?", and enumerating the rest adds lines without adding an answer. They do get accurate audiences on drill-down:

```
$ entire agent-help checkpoint --json
  explain  read-only     list   read-only    search  read-only
  tokens   read-only     policy task-driven
```

Which groups break out is declared in `agentHelpBreakoutGroups`, not inferred from "has classified children" — otherwise classifying some unrelated subcommand would silently change the listing. The CI guard now also requires every child of a breakout group to be classified, since an unclassified one would be silently withheld from the safe bucket, which is the exact failure the breakout exists to prevent.

## `review` and `investigate` moved

Both now sit in the user-owned bucket. I widened that heading's rationale to cover them, since they aren't setup or destructive — they're *expensive*: "setup, auth, admin, destructive, or expensive enough that starting one uninvited is the user's call."

`--json` omits `audience` entirely where the table makes no claim (e.g. `org create`), rather than emitting the user-owned default as if it were a deliberate classification.

## Verification

`fmt` + `lint` + `test:ci` — 8830 unit, 120 integration, 60 + 4 canary, all passing. The two `goconst` findings in `plugin_fetch.go` are still there and still pre-existing on `main`; my offer stands to either fix them on this branch or leave them for a separate one.

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF' && git log --oneline -1
feat(agent-help): group commands by who should initiate them; trim the injection

Two changes, both aimed at the same thing: tell agents what they may run on
their own, in the place they actually read.

The first-turn injection recommended `entire why <file>:<line>` and `entire
checkpoint search` "before large edits". A census of 963 agent transcripts on a
heavy-use machine (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Factory, Gemini, opencode, pi;
447k records, 12,275 shell calls) found ZERO invocations of either, against 25
calls to the `entire agent-help` pointer in the same corpus. The recommendation
only ever cost first-turn tokens, and it framed a sometimes-appropriate query as
an always-do step. It is gone; the injection now carries only invariants that
hold on every turn (auto-capture, setup/destructive belong to the user, the
auto-detected repo).

Which command suits a task belongs in agent-help, which is pulled on demand.
But agent-help was a flat alphabetical dump of 33 commands, which cannot answer
the only question an agent has when reading it: may I run this unprompted? It is
now grouped by initiator:

  read-only    safe on your own; changes nothing
  task-driven  writes data or spends tokens
  user-owned   setup, auth, admin, destructive, or expensive enough that
               starting one uninvited is the user's call

Notes on the classification, which lives in one reviewable table
(agentHelpAudiences, keyed by command path):

- A group is read-only only if EVERY advertised subcommand is. `checkpoint` and
  `session` read as read-only from their Short help but are not: `checkpoint
  policy` updates policy, and `session` carries adopt/attach/resume/stop.
- Demoting those groups would have hidden the inspection commands agents most
  want, so their read-only subcommands are classified individually and broken
  out into the read-only bucket (`checkpoint list`, `session list`, …). The
  groups that do this are declared in agentHelpBreakoutGroups rather than
  inferred, so classifying an unrelated subcommand cannot silently change the
  listing.
- `review` and `investigate` are user-owned: they spawn paid multi-agent runs,
  so starting one uninvited is the user's call.
- Unclassified commands default to user-owned — the fail-safe direction is an
  agent declining to run something it could have. A CI guard fails when a new
  top-level command, or a new child of a breakout group, ships unclassified.

`--json` mirrors the grouping as an `audience` field so structured consumers get
the same guidance (the repo's agent-safe-fallback rule), and omits it where the
table makes no claim rather than emitting the default as if deliberate.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

input.command:
gh pr create --title "feat(agent-help): group commands by who should initiate them; trim the injection" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Two changes aimed at the same thing: tell agents what they may run on their own, in the place they actually read.

## Why: the injection's command recommendations were never used

The first-turn context injection urged `entire why <file>:<line>` and `entire checkpoint search` "before large edits". I measured whether that ever worked, across every agent transcript on a heavy-use machine — Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Factory, Gemini, opencode, pi: **963 transcripts, 447k records, 12,275 shell calls**.

| command | real invocations |
|---|---|
| `entire why` | **0** |
| `entire checkpoint search` | **0** |
| `entire agent-help` (the pointer above it) | 25 |

Counting is subtler than it looks: the injection quotes both commands verbatim into every prompt, and both appear in our own source, help output, and PR bodies — so a text grep is ~100% false positives. These numbers count only shell **command position** inside a tool call's command field, after stripping heredoc bodies and masking quoted spans.

So the recommendation only ever cost first-turn tokens, and it framed a sometimes-appropriate query as an always-do step. **It's removed.** The injection now carries only invariants that hold on every turn: commits auto-capture checkpoints, setup/destructive commands belong to the user, and the auto-detected repo name.

## What replaces it: agent-help grouped by initiator

Which command suits a task belongs in `agent-help`, which is pulled on demand. But `agent-help` was a flat alphabetical dump of 33 commands, which can't answer the only question an agent has when reading it — *may I run this unprompted?*

```
  Safe to run on your own — read-only, changes nothing:
    activity  blame  checkpoint explain  checkpoint list  checkpoint search
    checkpoint tokens  experts  labs  recap  search  session current
    session info  session list  session tokens  status  tokens  version  why

  Run when the task calls for it — some subcommands write data or spend tokens:
    api  checkpoint  dispatch  doctor  import  runner  session  trail

  The user's to run — suggest it, don't run it:
    agent  auth  clean  configure  disable  enable  grant  investigate
    login  logout  org  plugin  project  repo  review
```

Ordering is load-bearing: what an agent may do on its own first, what it must leave alone last.

## Classification notes (the reviewable part)

It lives in one table, `agentHelpAudiences`, keyed by command path.

- **A group is read-only only if _every_ advertised subcommand is.** `checkpoint` and `session` read as read-only from their `Short` help but are not: `checkpoint policy` is "Inspect and **update**", and `session` carries `adopt/attach/resume/stop`. Both are task-driven. There's a regression test naming both — I had them in read-only first.
- **Demoting those groups would have hidden the inspection commands agents most want**, so their read-only subcommands are classified individually and broken out into the read-only bucket. Which groups do this is *declared* (`agentHelpBreakoutGroups`), not inferred from "has classified children" — otherwise classifying some unrelated subcommand would silently change the listing.
- **`review` and `investigate` are user-owned.** They aren't setup or destructive, they're *expensive*: both spawn paid multi-agent runs, so starting one uninvited is the user's call.
- **Unclassified commands default to user-owned.** The fail-safe direction is an agent declining to run something it could have, never running something it shouldn't. `TestAgentHelpAudiences_CoverEveryAdvertisedCommand` fails CI when a new top-level command — or a new child of a breakout group — ships unclassified.

`--json` mirrors the grouping as an `audience` field so structured consumers get the same guidance (the repo's agent-safe-fallback rule), and omits it where the table makes no claim rather than emitting the default as if it were deliberate:

```
$ entire agent-help checkpoint --json
  explain read-only   list read-only   search read-only   tokens read-only
  policy  task-driven
```

## Testing

`mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test:ci` — lint **0 issues**, 8830 unit tests, 120 integration, 60 + 4 e2e canary, all green. New coverage: audience completeness guard, the mutating-subcommand honesty guard, section grouping and ordering, JSON audience emission, and a regression test pinning the injection trim.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -3

content.text:
Four real findings. Ranked.

## 1. [High] The breakout skipped the one family that actually gets used

The census that justifies this PR: `trail` **185 invocations**, `checkpoint` 6, `session` 1. I broke out read-only subcommands for the two least-used families and left the most-used one flat:

```
trail show        Show a trail            ← read-only
trail list        List recent trails      ← read-only
trail approvals   List approval decisions ← read-only
trail watch       Tail a trail's events   ← read-only
```

All four now sit behind a `trail → task-driven` label reading *"writes data or spends tokens."* Before this PR the listing was flat and said nothing; now it actively discourages the read-only commands in the highest-traffic family. That's a plausible behavior regression, and it inverts the PR's own stated goal.

Fix: add `trail` to `agentHelpBreakoutGroups` and classify its 13 children (4 read-only, 9 task-driven).

## 2. [Medium] The text drill-down silently drops what `--json` carries

```
$ entire agent-help checkpoint
Subcommands: explain · list · policy · search · tokens     ← no audience

$ entire agent-help checkpoint --json
explain read-only … policy task-driven                     ← audience present
```

An agent drilling in via text — the default path — cannot tell `policy` from `list`. This breaks the repo's own agent-safe-fallback rule ("plain text output is acceptable when it contains the full information needed"), which my own test comment cites while the code violates it. Self-inflicted in this PR.

## 3. [Medium] Half the documented rule has no CI guard

The rule is "a group is read-only only if every advertised subcommand is." `TestAgentHelpAudiences_CoverEveryAdvertisedCommand` enforces classification for top-level commands and breakout-group children — but not for **read-only groups**. Live instance:

```
tokens          → classified read-only
tokens profile  → unclassified, no audience in --json
```

Benign today (`profile` really is read-only), but a future `tokens purge` would inherit the "changes nothing" heading with nothing failing. That is precisely the failure mode the guard exists to prevent, on the branch of the rule I didn't cover.

## 4. [Low] The evidence is stated more broadly than it is

`CLAUDE.md` now permanently records "A census of 963 agent transcripts found zero invocations…" without noting it is **one machine, one developer (you)**. The PR body says "a heavy-use machine"; the repo docs don't. Related: zero invocations proves agents never *ran* the commands, not that the recommendation had no effect — I can't distinguish "never read" from "read and correctly judged inapplicable." Neither weakens the decision (the token cost and the always-do framing are real regardless), but the docs assert it as settled general fact.

## One thing I checked that is *not* a bug

`checkpoint policy` is experimental and hidden in stable builds, which would make every *advertised* child of `checkpoint` read-only there — seemingly contradicting the task-driven label. It isn't: per `CLAUDE.md`, experimental gating controls visibility only and the command stays runnable. Task-driven is correct in both builds.

---

Findings 1–3 are all in code I wrote in this PR, and 1 is worth fixing before merge. Want me to push fixes for 1–3 (and soften the CLAUDE.md wording for 4), or leave the PR as-is and file them?

content.text:
You're right, and it's worse than it looks: my own finding #1 would have made it worse. Adding `trail`'s breakout means +4 more lines, and every future group with mixed subcommands adds more. The listing is now 45 lines. I optimized "is this answer complete?" when the real constraint is "will an agent read this and act?"

The deeper mistake: I encoded a 2-D matrix (command × safety) as a flat list, so completeness costs a line per cell. Two fixes fall out of that, and they compose.

**Collapse the safety split back onto the group line** — one line instead of five, and it kills finding #2 as a side effect:

```
  checkpoint   Inspect checkpoints — explain/list/search/tokens read-only; policy writes
```

**Stop listing what the agent must not run.** 15 of 33 entries are user-owned. Spending 15 lines to say "don't" is backwards — one sentence says it better.

Here's the whole thing at that shape:

```
When to use entire — what's useful mid-task:

  status       Where Entire stands in this repo                       read-only
  trail        Branch trails — show/list/approvals/watch read-only;
               create/update/delete/approve/comment/… write
  checkpoint   Inspect checkpoints — explain/list/search/tokens
               read-only; policy writes
  session      Agent sessions — current/info/list/tokens read-only;
               adopt/attach/resume/stop write
  why          Why a line exists                                      read-only
  search       Search checkpoints, commits, sessions                  read-only
  api          Authenticated request to Entire's HTTP API             writes

Setup (enable, configure, auth), admin (org, project, repo, grant), and paid
multi-agent runs (review, investigate) are the user's to start — suggest them,
don't run them. `entire agent-help <command>` works for every command, listed
or not; `entire help` shows the full surface.
```

~12 lines against 45, and it answers *both* agent questions — is entire relevant here, and may I run it — without a taxonomy.

**On "hide behind deeper commands": yes, and the safety property is that nothing becomes unreachable.** `agent-help <cmd>` already resolves anything advertised, so curating the default view costs discoverability only for commands an agent shouldn't be initiating anyway. That satisfies the repo's agent-safe-fallback rule — the information is one explicit, signposted command away.

**The real risk is curation drift**: someone adds a genuinely agent-relevant command and it never appears. Mitigation is structural — make "listed" a field in the same CI-guarded table rather than a second list, so adding a command still forces the decision. The two questions are genuinely orthogonal (*shown?* and *safe?*), so that's a small struct rather than a wider enum — which is arguably the bug in my current design: I fused them into one axis and the listing inherited the fusion.

This does discard the `agentHelpBreakoutGroups` machinery from the open PR. I'd rather throw it away now than merge it and grow it.

One judgment call I'd want your read on: whether `review` and `investigate` belong in that trailing sentence or stay visible. You just moved them to user-owned on cost grounds, but they're also the commands a user is most likely to *name* ("run a review") — and an agent that can't see them may not connect the request to the command. My inclination is the sentence naming them explicitly is enough.

Want me to build this on the branch so you can see the real rendered output against the actual command tree, rather than my mock?

41	// agentHelpAudience answers the question an agent actually has when it reads this
42	// listing: may I run this without being asked? A flat alphabetical dump of every
43	// command cannot answer it, so an agent either runs nothing or runs something it
44	// should have left alone (`entire enable`, `entire review`, `entire org create`).
45	// Grouping by initiator puts that judgment in the CLI, where it is maintained
46	// once, rather than in each agent's guesswork or in the first-turn injection,
47	// which pays for it on every session.
48	type agentHelpAudience int
49	
50	const (
51		// agentHelpAudienceReadOnly: inspection only. Safe to run unprompted whenever
52		// it would inform the work; cannot change repo, account, or Entire state.
53		agentHelpAudienceReadOnly agentHelpAudience = iota
54		// agentHelpAudienceTaskDriven: part of doing the work, but it writes data or
55		// spends tokens. Run when the task calls for it, not speculatively.
56		agentHelpAudienceTaskDriven
57		// agentHelpAudienceUserOwned: setup, auth, account/admin, or destructive. The
58		// agent may suggest these but must not run them on its own initiative.
59		agentHelpAudienceUserOwned

62	// agentHelpAudiences classifies commands by space-separated path relative to the
63	// root ("status", "checkpoint list"). It is a single table rather than a
64	// per-command Annotations field so the whole policy is reviewable in one place —
65	// the classification is a judgment call and reads as one only when the commands
66	// sit side by side.
67	//
68	// A GROUP is read-only only if every advertised subcommand is, so `checkpoint`
69	// and `session` are task-driven even though their Short help reads as pure
70	// inspection: `checkpoint policy` updates policy, and `session` carries
71	// adopt/attach/resume/stop. Demoting the whole group would have hidden the
72	// inspection commands an agent most wants (`checkpoint list`, `session list`),
73	// so their read-only subcommands are classified individually and the listing
74	// breaks them out — see agentHelpEntries. The mutating siblings are classified
75	// too; they stay collapsed under the group in the listing but carry an accurate
76	// audience in `agent-help <group> --json`.
77	//
78	// Unlisted commands fall back to agentHelpAudienceUserOwned (see
79	// agentHelpAudienceFor): the fail-safe direction is an agent declining to run

input.old_string:
The bare listing is grouped by **who should initiate the command**, not
alphabetically, because the question an agent has when reading it is "may I run
this unprompted?" — read-only (safe on its own) · task-driven (writes data or
spends tokens) · user-owned (setup, auth, admin, destructive, or expensive
enough that starting one uninvited is the user's call — `review` and
`investigate` spawn paid multi-agent runs and live here). The classification
lives in one reviewable table, `agentHelpAudiences` in `agent_help_cmd.go`, keyed
by command path (`status`, `checkpoint list`), and is mirrored into `--json` as an
`audience` field so structured consumers get the same guidance.

Three rules matter when editing it:

- A group counts as read-only **only if every advertised subcommand is**.
  `checkpoint` and `session` read as read-only but are not (`checkpoint policy`
  updates policy; `session` carries adopt/attach/resume/stop), so both are
  task-driven.
- Because demoting those groups would hide the inspection commands agents most
  want, their read-only subcommands are classified individually and listed
  under read-only (`checkpoint list`, `session list`, …). The groups that do
  this are declared in `agentHelpBreakoutGroups` rather than inferred, and must
  classify **every** child.
- An unclassified command defaults to user-owned, and
  `TestAgentHelpAudiences_CoverEveryAdvertisedCommand` fails CI so neither a new
  top-level command nor a new subcommand of a breakout group can ship
  unclassified. `--json` omits `audience` where the table makes no claim rather
  than emitting that default.
input.new_string:
The bare listing shows a **curated subset**, not the whole tree. An exhaustive
listing answers "what exists?", which is not the question an agent mid-task has,
and past a certain length it stops being read at all — an earlier revision that
listed everything grouped by audience reached 45 lines. Omitted commands stay
reachable (`agent-help <command>` resolves them, and the footer names them in a
compact index), so curation trades default visibility, never availability.

`agentHelpClassification` in `agent_help_cmd.go` is the one reviewable table,
keyed by command path (`status`, `checkpoint list`). Each entry carries two
**independent** facts — fusing them into a single axis is what forced the
listing to spend a line per (command × audience) cell:

- `audience` — may an agent run this unprompted? read-only · task-driven
  (writes data or spends tokens) · user-owned (setup, auth, admin, destructive,
  or expensive enough that starting one uninvited is the user's call — `review`
  and `investigate` spawn paid multi-agent runs and live here). Applies at every
  depth; mirrored into `--json` as `audience`.
- `listed` — does it appear in the bare listing? Top-level commands only.

Rules when editing it:

- A group's audience is a claim about **all** its subcommands, so a read-only
  group may not contain one that writes. `checkpoint` and `session` read as
  read-only but are not (`checkpoint policy` updates policy; `session` carries
  adopt/attach/resume/stop), so both are task-driven.
- A mixed group states its exceptions **on one line**, naming only the minority
  side (`read-only except: policy`, or `read-only: show, list, … — others
  write`). That is what keeps a group at one line however many subcommands it
  grows. Both the text drill-down and `--json` carry this, so neither mode hides
  which subcommands write.
- An unclassified command defaults to user-owned and unlisted.
  `TestAgentHelpClassification_CoversEveryAdvertisedCommand` fails CI so neither
  a new top-level command nor a new child of a *listed* group can ship
  unclassified — an unclassified child would be silently dropped from its
  group's exception note. `--json` omits `audience` where the table makes no
  claim rather than emitting the default.

refactor(agent-help): curate the listing instead of enumerating everything

The grouped listing from the previous commit was more complete and less
useful. Grouping every command by audience meant spending a line per
(command × audience) cell, so it reached 45 lines — and the fix for the
review finding about `trail` would have added four more. Completeness and
readability were pulling against each other because the model fused two
independent questions into one axis.

Split them. agentHelpFacts now carries:

  audience — may I run this unprompted?      (every command, any depth)
  listed   — worth showing by default?       (top-level only)

The bare listing shows the seven commands that bear on an agent's work
mid-task (status, why, search, api, checkpoint, session, trail). Everything
else is named in a compact footer index — enough for an agent to connect
"run a review" to a command, without an entry apiece. Nothing becomes
unreachable: `agent-help <command>` still resolves every advertised command,
so this trades default visibility, not availability.

A mixed group now states its exceptions on ONE line, naming only the
minority side:

  checkpoint  Inspect and search checkpoints
                read-only except: policy
  trail       Manage trails for your branches
                read-only: approvals, list, show, watch — others write

That holds at one line however many subcommands a group grows, which the
per-subcommand breakout it replaces did not.

Also fixes three findings from the adversarial review of the previous
commit:

- trail, the highest-traffic family by a wide margin, had no breakout at
  all, so its four read-only subcommands sat behind a write-capable label.
  All 13 are now classified and the group names its read-only side.
- The text drill-down dropped the audience that --json carried, so an agent
  drilling in via text could not tell `checkpoint list` from `checkpoint
  policy`. Both modes now carry it.
- "A read-only group has no writing children" was documented but only
  enforced for breakout groups, leaving `tokens`/`tokens profile`
  unguarded. A test now checks every read-only group, and the completeness
  guard covers every child of a listed group.

Pushed to PR #1967. Your instinct was right, and it also killed three of my four review findings as a side effect.

## What the listing looks like now — 32 lines, down from 45

```
When to use entire — the commands that bear on the work:
  api         Make an authenticated request to an Entire API and print the response
                task-driven
  checkpoint  Inspect and search checkpoints
                read-only except: policy
  search      Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching
                read-only
  session     Manage agent sessions tracked by Entire
                read-only except: adopt, attach, resume, stop
  status      Show Entire status
                read-only
  trail       Manage trails for your branches
                read-only: approvals, list, show, watch — others write
  why         Show why a line exists
                read-only

Also available — setup, admin, and commands to run only when asked:
  activity · agent · auth · blame · clean · configure · disable
  dispatch · doctor · enable · experts · grant · import · investigate
  labs · login · logout · org · plugin · project · recap · repo
  review · runner · tokens · version
  Suggest these; don't run them uninvited.
```

**The root cause was the model, not the rendering.** I'd fused two independent questions into one axis, which forced a line per (command × audience) cell. Splitting them into `audience` (every command, any depth) and `listed` (top-level only) makes the size problem go away structurally rather than by trimming text.

**The one-line exception note is what makes it scale.** Naming only the minority side keeps a group at one line no matter how many subcommands it grows — where the breakout it replaces cost a line each. That's why adding all 13 `trail` subcommands *shrank* the output.

## Review findings, resolved

- **#1 `trail` had no breakout** — all 13 subcommands classified; the group now names its read-only side. This was the finding that would have made the old design worse.
- **#2 text drill-down hid what `--json` showed** — both modes now carry the note.
- **#3 read-only-group rule unenforced** — a test now checks *every* read-only group for writing children, and the completeness guard covers every child of a listed group. `tokens profile` is classified rather than assumed.
- **#4 overstated evidence in CLAUDE.md** — still open; I left the wording alone since you didn't weigh in, and it's a docs-only edit I can make in a moment.

## Two things worth flagging

I made a real mess mid-way: a range-based replacement over-reached and deleted `newAgentHelpCmd`, `runAgentHelp`, and the JSON types. I caught it on the build, restored from the commit, and redid it with targeted edits — no trace in the pushed result, but it cost time and I should have used narrow edits from the start.

Lint also caught two issues in my own new code (a non-exhaustive `switch` and a repeated `"user-owned"` literal). Both fixed; the exhaustive fix now degrades an unknown future enum member to `user-owned` rather than something agent-runnable.

`fmt` + `lint` (**0 issues**) + `test:ci` all green. CI is running on the PR — want me to watch it again, and do you want the CLAUDE.md sampling caveat added?

Pushed. Two things, since unlisting turned out to be the sharper end of your point.

## `entire api` now says what it's for

```
entire api — Escape hatch: authenticated raw request to an Entire API

THIS IS A LAST RESORT. It is the right tool in two cases:
  - you are developing against Entire's own APIs and want to inspect a
    raw response, or
  - no first-class command covers what you need.

Otherwise prefer the command built for the job — `entire checkpoint`,
`entire session`, `entire trail`, `entire status`, `entire repo`, and so on.
They return stable, documented output; raw endpoints are internal and can
change shape without notice, so parsing them is brittle. If you find
yourself reaching for `entire api` during ordinary work in a repo that has
Entire enabled, check `entire agent-help` first — there is probably a
command for it.

When you do need it, use this rather than hand-rolling curl: …
```

I also **removed it from the curated listing**, which your wording implies more strongly than "add an explanation" does — if it's usually not the use case, it doesn't belong in the set of commands that bear on the work. Front line is now six: `checkpoint`, `search`, `session`, `status`, `trail`, `why`.

**The balance I was careful not to break:** `CLAUDE.md` advertises `api` specifically so agents don't hand-roll curl with a token. So it stays visible in `entire help` and named in agent-help's footer — discoverable when genuinely needed, just not suggested by default. I wrote that trade-off into `CLAUDE.md` so a future change doesn't silently pick one side.

## Unlisting exposed a bug I'd introduced

The footer had one bucket captioned *"Suggest these; don't run them uninvited."* That's false for the read-only commands sitting in it — `activity`, `blame`, `experts`, `labs`, `recap`, `tokens`, `version` — and it directly contradicted the audience table, which calls them safe unprompted. A single bucket has to caption itself with its most restrictive member.

Split by audience, still names-only:

```
Also available (entire agent-help <command> for any of these):
  read-only, safe to run:
    activity · blame · experts · labs · recap · tokens · version
  when the task needs them:
    api · dispatch · doctor · import · runner
  the user's — suggest, don't run:
    agent · auth · clean · configure · disable · enable · grant
    investigate · login · logout · org · plugin · project · repo
    review
```

33 lines total — one more than before, buying accuracy. There's a test pinning that read-only commands never fall under the do-not-run caption.

`fmt` + `lint` (0 issues) + `test:ci` all green. Still open from the earlier review: the `CLAUDE.md` sampling caveat (finding #4) — one-line edit whenever you want it.

`api` is an **escape hatch, not a front-line command**, and its help says so.
It is the right tool in exactly two cases: developing against Entire's own APIs
and wanting a raw response, or needing something no first-class command covers.
Otherwise the purpose-built command wins — raw endpoints are internal and can
change shape without notice, so parsing them is brittle. It is therefore
deliberately **not** in `agent-help`'s curated listing (`listed: false`), but
stays visible in `entire help` and named in agent-help's footer index so an
agent that genuinely needs raw access finds it instead of hand-rolling curl
with a token — which is the failure this command exists to prevent. Keep both
halves of that balance in mind when changing its visibility.

developing against Entire's own APIs and wanting a raw response, or when no
first-class command covers the need — not during ordinary work in a repo with
Entire enabled. It is therefore deliberately **not** in `agent-help`'s curated

**Where that steer lives matters.** "This is a last resort" is agent guidance,
not human help: someone who typed `entire api --help` chose the command on
purpose, and telling them to reconsider is noise. So it lives in

cobra's `Long`. The split rule, which applies to any command that needs it:

- true for **both** audiences → `Long` (e.g. "these endpoints are internal and
  can change shape without notice")
- useful only to an agent choosing from a surface it doesn't know →
  `agentHelpGuidance`

content.text:
Fixed — that was the right call, and it generalizes into a rule rather than a one-off.

## Human help is a reference again

```
$ entire api --help
Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host…
```

`Short` is restored verbatim, so `entire help` reads normally too.

## The steer moved to the agent channel

```
$ entire agent-help api
…
When to use this:
LAST RESORT. Right in two cases: you are developing against Entire's own
APIs and want a raw response, or no first-class command covers your need.
Otherwise prefer the command built for the job (checkpoint, session, trail,
status, repo, …) — its output is stable, raw endpoints are not. …
```

New `agentHelpGuidance` map, keyed by command path like the classification table. Rendered by `agent-help` *before* flags and examples — whether to use a command outranks how to call it — and as a `guidance` field in `--json`.

## The general rule I wrote down

The interesting part is *why* the two audiences differ, because it decides where any future steer goes:

- **True for both** → cobra's `Long`. "These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice" is a compatibility fact, so humans keep it.
- **Only useful to an agent picking from a surface it doesn't know** → `agentHelpGuidance`.

A human who typed the command already made the choice; an agent hasn't. Same sentence, opposite value.

`TestAgentHelpGuidance_NeverLeaksIntoCobraHelp` walks every guidance entry and fails CI if its first line appears in that command's `Short` or `Long` — so this can't drift back. The `api` test also asserts positively that the human help *lacks* "LAST RESORT" and *keeps* the stability caveat.

`fmt` + `lint` (0 issues) + `test:ci` all green; pushed to PR #1967.

Still outstanding, whenever you want it: the `CLAUDE.md` sampling caveat from finding #4 (noting the census was one machine, one developer).
